To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

people’s judgments of causality are influenced by the amount of delay variability between a cause and its effect, and that this is because people are sensitive to the amount of time that has passed since the cause occurred.

(1) participants’ causal judgments were influenced by delay variability, and (2) participants’ causal ratings of cause-effect pairs were influenced by the number of intervening events in a causeeffect interval rather than the length or variability of the interval itself.

(1) delay variability, but not delay length per se, influences people’s causal judgments; and (2) participants’ sensitivity to variability can be explained in terms either of a sensitivity to the presence of an active hastener, or a sensitivity to intervening events.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of temporal information on causal judgments.
how people use time to inform their causal judgements.
how people learn causal relations from experience.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the findings of this thesis have implications for current theories of causal induction.
The results from Experiments 1 and 2 show that participants’ causal judgments are influenced by the delay between cause-effect events.
the results of this study suggest that the influence of delay on causal judgments is complex, and may depend on a number of factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the delay in the causal relationship has a significant effect on causal judgments.

people are very sensitive to the variability in delays between causes and their effects, but that they are also sensitive to other factors that influence the delay, such as the presence of a cue that hastens the effect, or the presence of intervening events.
people use the temporal structure of an event to inform their causal inferences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people are highly sensitive to the variability of delays in their causal judgments, but that this sensitivity is not limited to the length of the delay.
the causal learning literature needs a more sophisticated account of how delays are used to inform causal judgments.
people are sensitive to variability in delay and to the probability of intervening causes.
